themes.label: Default stance and who decides
themes.desc: Whether AI is allowed by default, who sets the rule (department, instructor, assignment), and whether uses are sorted into levels or categories.

themes.label: Communicating expectations
themes.desc: How and where the rules are made explicit to students.

themes.label: What students may use AI for
themes.desc: Uses that are allowed or encouraged: explanation, debugging help, brainstorming, writing support, course-provided tools.

themes.label: What students may not use AI for
themes.desc: Uses that are ruled out, especially generating code or solutions that are submitted as one's own.

themes.label: Disclosure and attribution
themes.desc: Whether and how AI use must be acknowledged, cited, or documented (prompts, transcripts, reflections).

themes.label: Student accountability and understanding
themes.desc: Students remain responsible for what they submit and must be able to explain and defend it.

themes.label: Assessment design
themes.desc: How assignments, exams, weighting, and formats change in response to AI.

themes.label: Detection and enforcement
themes.desc: Detectors, evidence, academic-integrity processes, sanctions, and amnesty.

themes.label: Why: learning and careers
themes.desc: The reasons given: protecting skill-building and productive struggle, and preparing students for AI-rich professional work.

themes.label: Faculty and staff use of AI
themes.desc: AI use by instructors and TAs for grading, feedback, materials, and course operations.

themes.label: Equity, privacy, ethics, and IP
themes.desc: Access and cost, data and privacy, bias and environmental concerns, and intellectual property.

themes.label: Governance and change over time
themes.desc: Acknowledging that policy will change, review cycles, and who maintains the policy.

types.name: Prohibit AI on graded work by default
types.covers: The default rule bans generative AI on graded work (or on all work) in the course or unit.

types.name: Permit or encourage AI by default
types.covers: The default rule allows, welcomes, encourages, or expects generative AI use.

types.name: Discourage AI without forbidding it
types.covers: AI is discouraged or not recommended, but not formally prohibited.

types.name: Let each instructor or assignment set the rule
types.covers: Whether AI is allowed is decided per instructor, per assignment, or per activity rather than by one rule.

types.name: Name explicit tiers or levels of AI use
types.covers: The policy defines named tiers, levels, colors, or categories of permitted AI use (e.g. no AI / limited / open), or a table of uses per assessment.

types.name: Define the fallback rule when a syllabus is silent
types.covers: States what applies when a syllabus or assignment says nothing about AI (e.g. 'unless explicitly allowed, AI is prohibited').

types.name: Cover AI built into editors, IDEs, and agents
types.covers: Rules that cover AI built into editors and IDEs (Copilot, Cursor, autocomplete), operating systems, browsers, or autonomous coding agents, including requiring students to disable them.

types.name: Stage AI permission as skills develop
types.covers: AI permission changes over the course: forbidden early, allowed later once fundamentals are mastered or in later projects or advanced courses.

types.name: Require an AI statement in every syllabus
types.covers: Instructors or departments must state AI expectations in the syllabus or assignment instructions.

types.name: When unsure, students should ask before using AI
types.covers: Students who are unsure whether a use is allowed should ask the instructor first, or err on the side of not using AI.

types.name: Each course's policy governs only that course
types.covers: One course's AI permissions do not carry over to other courses or assignments.

types.name: Allow AI as a tutor for understanding concepts
types.covers: AI may be used like a tutor or search engine to understand concepts, lecture material, or general questions, not to produce graded answers.

types.name: Allow AI to explain errors and help debug
types.covers: AI may be used to explain error messages, help debug, or clarify syntax.

types.name: Allow AI for practice, study aids, and review
types.covers: AI may be used to generate practice problems, study guides, summaries, reviews, or self-checks of knowledge.

types.name: Allow AI for brainstorming and exploring approaches
types.covers: AI may be used for brainstorming, idea generation, or exploring alternative approaches.

types.name: Allow AI-generated code under stated conditions
types.covers: Students may submit or use AI-generated code under explicit conditions (small snippets, line or percentage caps, cited, specific projects, or freely).

types.name: Provide a sanctioned, course-specific AI tool
types.covers: The course or university provides its own sanctioned AI tool (a course chatbot, tutor bot, or licensed assistant), sometimes the only AI allowed.

types.name: Treat AI for prose separately from AI for code
types.covers: Specific rules for AI in prose and writing (reports, essays, comments, grammar or translation tools), separate from code.

types.name: Do not have AI produce the work you submit
types.covers: Students may not have AI generate the code, solutions, text, or answers they submit as their own.

types.name: Do not feed assignment specs or your code to AI
types.covers: Students may not paste or upload assignment specifications, questions, their own code, or the codebase into an AI tool.

types.name: Do not use AI to debug or check graded work
types.covers: Students may not use AI to debug, fix, proofread, reformat, or check graded work.

types.name: No AI on exams, quizzes, or in-class assessments
types.covers: No AI on exams, quizzes, tests, or in-class assessments; closed-device rules during exams.

types.name: Keep AI conversations apart from the work itself
types.covers: Keep AI conversations separate from the work: close the AI before writing, never copy-paste from it, never have both open, or use only browser chat interfaces.

types.name: Disclose AI use with each submission
types.covers: Students must disclose, acknowledge, or cite any AI use in their submission (a statement or citation).

types.name: Cite the tool, the prompt, and the output
types.covers: Citations of AI must include specific details such as the tool or model, the exact prompt, the output, or the date.

types.name: Keep and submit transcripts, logs, or reflections
types.covers: Students must keep and submit full transcripts, chat logs, journals, drafts, or reflections on their AI use.

types.name: Mark AI-derived code where it is used
types.covers: AI-derived code must be marked at the exact place it is used (code comments, README, acknowledgments file, top of file).

types.name: Make disclosure safe and nondisclosure the violation
types.covers: How disclosure affects grading or integrity: disclosed use is not penalized, or failure to disclose is itself the violation (or, conversely, disclosed use is still penalized).

types.name: Students own everything they submit
types.covers: Students are responsible for and must own all work they submit; submitted work must be their own.

types.name: Students must be able to explain every line
types.covers: Students must understand and be able to explain or defend every line and part of what they submit.

types.name: Verify AI output; it is often wrong
types.covers: AI output can be wrong, biased, or hallucinated; students must verify and critically evaluate it.

types.name: Students stay the primary problem-solver
types.covers: Students should remain the primary thinker and decision-maker; AI must not replace their thinking.

types.name: Shift weight to proctored, unassisted assessment
types.covers: Assessment weight shifts toward proctored, in-class, or unassisted evaluation because of AI.

types.name: Check understanding through code reviews, interviews, or oral exams
types.covers: Understanding is checked through code reviews, interviews, oral exams, demos, or meetings where students explain their work.

types.name: Redesign assignments and grading around AI
types.covers: Assignments, grading schemes, or course structure are redesigned around AI (e.g. two-pass submissions, grading on process or hours, baselines for declared AI use). Includes assignment-specific AI interaction protocols, e.g. a required prompt header (UIUC CS 128).

types.name: Treat unauthorized AI use as academic misconduct
types.covers: Unauthorized or improper AI use is classified as academic misconduct, plagiarism, or cheating and handled by integrity processes.

types.name: State concrete penalties in advance
types.covers: Specific penalties for AI misuse are stated (zero, negative score, letter-grade reduction, course failure, escalation by offense).

types.name: Offer a self-report window or amnesty
types.covers: Students can self-report, withdraw a submission, or come forward within a window for reduced consequences.

types.name: Do not rely on AI detectors
types.covers: AI detectors are unreliable or will not be used or relied upon as proof.

types.name: Use similarity checks and process evidence instead
types.covers: Similarity checking, plagiarism software, AI-detection tools, commit histories, or activity logs are used to identify misuse.

types.name: Explain that AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill
types.covers: AI use is limited because doing the work yourself builds skill; outsourcing practice undermines learning.

types.name: Protect novices; fundamentals come first
types.covers: Beginners and foundational courses especially need to learn fundamentals without AI; novices cannot judge AI output.

types.name: Warn that AI gives a false sense of mastery
types.covers: Relying on AI creates a false sense of mastery that is exposed on exams or later work.

types.name: Teach effective AI use as a professional skill
types.covers: Learning to use AI effectively is a professional skill employers expect; courses teach or demonstrate AI use.

types.name: Treat AI like a human collaborator under existing rules
types.covers: AI is treated like a human collaborator, peer, or outside source under existing collaboration or citation rules.

types.name: Humans, not AI, assign grades
types.covers: Grades must be assigned by human instructors; AI will not grade or determine grades.

types.name: Disclose instructor AI use to students
types.covers: Instructors disclose or describe their own use of AI (in grading, feedback, demos, or communication) to students, or commit to limits on it.

types.name: Review and disclose AI-made course materials
types.covers: Course materials created with AI are disclosed and reviewed by instructors.

types.name: Do not upload course materials to AI tools
types.covers: Students may not upload course materials, assignment descriptions, or protected works into AI tools.

types.name: Protect personal data and prefer vetted tools
types.covers: Protect personal and confidential data; AI tools store prompts; prefer university-vetted or licensed tools.

types.name: Do not require paid tools; keep access equitable
types.covers: Equity and access: AI is optional or not required, free access is provided, paid tools are not required, accommodations and alternatives exist.

types.name: Consider licensing and copyright of AI output
types.covers: Copyright, licensing, terms of use, and ownership of AI inputs and outputs.

types.name: Name bias, harms, and environmental costs
types.covers: Ethical, bias, labor, and environmental concerns about AI.

types.name: Revisit the policy regularly
types.covers: The policy is provisional and will be revisited, revised, or updated; feedback is invited.

types.name: Gather evidence on how AI affects learning
types.covers: Evidence or data about how AI use affects student learning or performance is collected or cited.

types.name: Set an institution-wide framework for responsible AI use
types.covers: An institution-level framework or preamble stating the purpose, scope, and principles for AI use.

types.name: Talk with the student before escalating suspected misuse
types.covers: Instructors should talk with the student and gather context before escalating suspected AI misuse.

types.name: Students write their own course communication
types.covers: Messages, emails or posts that students send to course staff must be written by the student, not generated by AI (source: UC Irvine ICS 33/H32).

types.name: Instructor use of AI for teaching work
types.covers: What instructors or staff may, should or should not use AI for in their own teaching work: drafting syllabi, rubrics, quiz items, examples, feedback drafts, translations, letters. Final grading decisions are P46; disclosure to students is P47; AI-made course materials are P48 (sources: UIUC CITL and Grainger; Oregon State EECS).

types.name: Decline to police AI use
types.covers: Staff state they will not actively police or detect AI use, relying instead on unassisted assessments or student responsibility (source: UIUC ECE 220).

types.name: Define AI and the policy's scope
types.covers: Definitions of AI, generative AI, AI tools or agentic systems that set what a policy covers (sources: Oregon State, Howard).

types.name: Govern AI use in research and scholarship
types.covers: AI rules for theses, dissertations, manuscripts, grants and peer review, including deferring to venue, funder, sponsor or IRB rules (sources: Oregon State EECS, Howard Policy 100-022).

types.name: Support faculty in learning AI
types.covers: Workshops, consultations, faculty communities, and advice that instructors try AI tools and learn their implications before setting course policy (sources: Oregon State, Howard).

types.name: Students may respond to AI-misuse allegations
types.covers: Students accused of AI misuse have a right to respond or present evidence; fairness and transparency in AI-related integrity cases (source: Howard).

types.name: Review and approve AI tools, vendors and data sharing
types.covers: Institutional review of AI contracts and partnerships, and limits on licensing or sharing university data and IP with AI providers (source: Howard Policy 100-022). Broadened 2026-10-26 (D33): also covers review and approval of any AI tool or system before purchase or deployment (security, risk, accessibility, legal), and periodic re-evaluation of approved tools. Evidence: Morehouse, Old Dominion, Rutgers (3), Santa Clara, Oakland, Penn State, Northwestern, Purdue.

types.name: Explain and discuss the AI rules with students
types.covers: Instructors give students the reasons behind their AI rules, discuss AI in class, or word the rules with care (tone, avoiding anthropomorphic language), going beyond listing the rule in the syllabus. Evidence before adding: Carleton, Brown, Boston College, Case Western, IU Indianapolis, Binghamton, George Mason, Michigan State.

types.name: Co-create the AI policy with students
types.covers: Instructors set the course's AI expectations together with students, for example through class discussion, to build understanding and buy-in. Evidence: Cal Poly Pomona, Cal State LA, Georgetown, Georgia State.

types.name: Respond to misuse educatively, not only punitively
types.covers: Treat suspected or confirmed AI misuse, especially first offenses, as a learning opportunity; prefer educative or remedial responses; presume good faith; reduce the pressures that lead to cheating. Different from P60 (declining to police) and P57 (talking before escalating). Evidence: Austin CC, East Tennessee State, Florida State, IU Indianapolis, George Washington, Clemson, Case Western.

types.name: Set evidence standards for AI-misuse findings
types.covers: What evidence is needed, or not sufficient, to find AI misuse: a standard of proof, the kinds of evidence to weigh, or the statement that a hunch that work 'does not sound like the student' is not enough. Evidence: Cornell, Grinnell, Iowa State, Clark, Georgetown. Broadened 2026-10-26 (D33): also covers rules that detector output may be used only as supporting evidence, not as proof. Evidence: Oberlin, Rice, Santa Clara, Old Dominion, Rowan.

types.name: Provide or require AI training for students and staff
types.covers: The institution offers or mandates AI-literacy training, modules, guides or curricular AI-literacy for students, staff or the whole community. Faculty-only support is P63. Evidence: Georgia Southern, Kennesaw State, Clark, East Tennessee State, Florida International, Brown, Baylor, Cleveland State.

types.name: Report AI incidents, data exposure and misuse
types.covers: A duty or channel to report AI-related problems: accidental exposure of sensitive data, tool malfunctions, policy violations or misconduct by others. Evidence: Augusta, Case Western, Georgia State, Kansas State, Marquette.

types.name: Point students to human help alongside AI
types.covers: Students are directed to instructors, librarians, writing centers, advisors or other human support, alongside or instead of AI tools. Evidence: Marquette, Harvey Mudd, Cal State, Florida International, BYU, Clemson.

types.name: Keep humans responsible for decisions about people
types.covers: AI may not be the sole basis for consequential decisions about individuals, such as hiring, admissions, discipline, evaluation or academic standing; a human reviews and decides. Grading alone is P46. Evidence: Austin CC, Clark, Colby, Hampton, Michigan State.

types.name: Ban deceptive, fabricated or malicious AI use
types.covers: General conduct rules against using AI to deceive, impersonate, fabricate or falsify data or records, harass, spread misinformation, write malware or breach security. Evidence: Cal State, East Tennessee State, George Mason, Kansas State, LSU, Michigan State, Colby.

types.name: Guard against AI-enabled phishing and security threats
types.covers: Security awareness: watch for AI-crafted phishing, scams and deepfakes, and report suspicious messages. Evidence: Bowdoin, Bucknell, Colby, East Carolina, Georgia Tech, Howard, Lamar.

types.name: Govern administrative and operational AI use
types.covers: Rules for AI in university operations outside teaching, such as staff administrative work, student services, official communications, chatbots or AI-built apps shared with others. Evidence: Brandeis, Hampton, Davidson, Kansas State, DePaul, Cal State.

types.name: Comply with existing law and university policy
types.covers: AI use must follow laws (records, privacy, IP) and existing university policies (conduct, acceptable use, branding), and violations fall under those policies. Different from P45, which treats AI like a human collaborator under integrity rules. Evidence: Amherst, Boise State, Kansas State, Arizona State, Cal State, Davidson.

types.name: Students learn and follow each course's AI rules
types.covers: Students are responsible for finding out, reading and following the AI rules that apply to them in each course, program or assignment (check the syllabus first). Different from P10 (ask when unsure) and P11 (a course's rule binds only that course). Evidence: Georgetown, Harvey Mudd, Rutgers-Camden, Rutgers-Newark, Princeton, Oakland, San José State, NIU, Northwestern, NAU, Portland State.

types.name: Require AI use in some coursework
types.covers: AI use is built into, expected in or required for an assignment or course, or instructors are told they may require it. Evidence: Ohio State, RIT, Brown, Oregon State, Pepperdine, Oakland, Northeastern, Sam Houston State.

types.name: Name who owns, enforces and grants exceptions to the AI policy
types.covers: Names the office, officer, council or committee that interprets, implements, monitors or enforces the AI policy, or the process for granting exceptions to it. Evidence: Purdue, Rowan, Oakland, Morehouse, Northeastern, Northwestern, Portland State, Santa Clara.

types.name: Follow the formal integrity-reporting procedure
types.covers: Procedural steps once misuse is suspected or sanctioned: instructors file a report with a central office, meet deadlines, use a required form, and leave sanctions to the deciding body. Different from P36 (classifying misuse as misconduct) and P57 (talking with the student first). Evidence: San José State, RPI, Rowan, SMU, Santa Clara, Oregon State, Rice, Oberlin, Portland State.

types.name: Acknowledge that AI use cannot be fully prevented or verified
types.covers: States limits on control: bans are impractical or counterproductive, AI use cannot be fully eliminated, faculty cannot always verify originality, assessments lose reliability. Evidence: Rush, NC A&T, Oregon State, RIT, MIT, NC State.

types.name: Align AI decisions with learning objectives
types.covers: Whether and how AI is allowed should follow from the course's or program's learning objectives. Evidence: Rush, Northeastern, Case Western, SF State, Morehouse, Santa Clara, Middle Tennessee State.

types.name: Describe how and by whom the policy was made
types.covers: States the process, body or date by which the AI policy or guidance was drafted, consulted on, adopted or ratified. Evidence: New Mexico State, Rice, Northeastern, Santa Clara.

types.name: Let schools or units set their own AI rules
types.covers: Colleges, schools, departments or programs may set their own or additional AI rules, or have different expectations from the university-wide rule. P04 is the instructor-level version. Evidence: Santa Clara, Saint Louis, Northeastern, San Diego State, Purdue, Middle Tennessee State, SMU.

types.name: Require consent before AI recording or transcription
types.covers: Class sessions or meetings may not be recorded or transcribed by AI tools without permission or announcement. Evidence: Augusta, Kean, Oregon State, Santa Clara.

types.name: State the benefits of AI for learning
types.covers: Names benefits of AI for teaching and learning (personalization, accessibility, efficiency, creativity) without making it a rule or a career-skill claim (P44). Evidence: New Mexico State, LSU, Ohio State, NC State, Prairie View A&M, Rush, SF State.

types.name: Engage peers, partners and the community on AI
types.covers: Coalitions with other universities, benchmarking against peers, partnerships with industry or government, and public forums on AI. Evidence: Brown, EVMS, Kansas State, Old Dominion.

types.name: Allow AI for data analysis and visualization
types.covers: AI may be used to analyze, sort, simulate or visualize data. Evidence: Ohio State, Morehouse, FIU, SMU, NAU, Sam Houston State.

types.name: Do the work yourself first, then use AI
types.covers: A sequencing rule: the student first attempts, drafts or develops the work without AI, and AI help is allowed only afterward. Evidence: Ohio State, North Dakota State, Oregon State, Northwestern.

types.name: Allow AI for editing, proofreading and writing support
types.covers: AI may help with editing, proofreading, grammar, outlining, organizing or revising one's own writing. P18 is about treating prose differently from code; this is the permission itself. Evidence: Morehouse, Rutgers, NAU, Ohio State, Oakland, Rowan, Penn State, Rush, NC State.

types.name: Use university-licensed or approved AI tools
types.covers: Use the AI tools the university licenses, provides or approves (institution-wide, not one course: that is P17), or know the approved list. Evidence: NYU, Morehouse, Rutgers (3 campuses), SUNY ESF, RIT, Nova Southeastern, Rowan, NC State.

types.name: Advise on how to prompt AI effectively
types.covers: Practical advice on writing prompts or probing AI tools to get better results or learn their limits. Evidence: Pepperdine, Oakland, Sam Houston State, Santa Clara, San Diego State, NC State.

types.name: Cite careers as a reason to build skills without AI
types.covers: The reason given for limiting AI is professional readiness: employers expect skills, critical thinking or work in settings without AI. P44 is the opposite argument (learn AI for careers). Evidence: Oregon State, RIT, Santa Clara, Princeton.

types.name: Ground AI limits in fairness and academic honesty
types.covers: The reason given for AI rules is fairness to other students, honest evaluation, or the integrity culture of the community, not skill-building (P41). Evidence: CUNY Graduate Center, Santa Clara, Prairie View A&M, Northeastern Illinois, San José State, Oberlin.

types.name: Treat AI as neither author, source nor collaborator
types.covers: AI is not a person: it cannot be an author, a cited source or a group member, and AI use is not acceptable collaboration. The opposite of P45. Evidence: Princeton, Pepperdine, Santa Clara.

types.name: Make AI use and output accessible
types.covers: Accessibility of AI tools and AI-produced materials for people with disabilities: accessibility reviews, alternative access plans, accessible output, AI as an accessibility aid. P51 covers cost and equal access. Evidence: Nova Southeastern, Ohio State, Penn State, Oregon State, Santa Clara, NAU.

types.name: Document, audit and monitor deployed AI systems
types.covers: Institutional AI systems are documented (model cards, records), audited or monitored for bias, accuracy, security and drift over time. Evidence: Morehouse, Georgia Southern, Old Dominion, Saint Louis, Oakland, Northwestern.

types.name: Reduce the pressures that lead to AI misuse
types.covers: Prevention by easing the causes of misuse: extensions, office hours, support resources, time management, explaining assignment purposes. P68 is the response after misuse. Evidence: Clemson, Rice, Old Dominion, IU Indianapolis, BYU.

types.name: Exempt routine AI features from the rules
types.covers: Routine embedded features (spell-check, grammar check, search, autocomplete) are allowed or need no disclosure even under a restrictive rule. Evidence: Oregon State, Morehouse, Pepperdine.

types.name: Set conditions for AI-assisted grading
types.covers: AI-assisted grading or feedback is allowed only under conditions: approval chains, explainability, human review of AI-drafted feedback, closed-form only. P46 is the rule that only humans assign grades. Evidence: Penn State, Purdue, Northeastern, SMU, Old Dominion, Oregon State.

types.name: Stay informed about AI developments and guidance
types.covers: A duty or encouragement for users to keep up with AI developments, best practices and the institution's current AI guidance. Evidence: East Tennessee State, San Diego State, NAU.

types.name: Tell people when they are interacting with AI
types.covers: People have a right to know when they are dealing with an AI system (chatbots, deployed systems), including its scope and limits. P47 is instructor disclosure to students. Evidence: Northwestern, Cal State, Morehouse.
